title: Prisoner's Dilemma: The Game Every Cross-Team Project Is Secretly Playing
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss applies classic game theory to a familiar engineering-management failure mode: two teams that agree on a shared spec but quietly build workarounds instead, each assuming the other will miss the deadline, ship bugs, or change the interface unannounced. Tracing the framework to RAND Corporation researchers studying Cold War nuclear strategy in the 1950s, the piece walks through the four possible outcomes of the classic Prisoner's Dilemma and maps them onto a concrete cross-team scenario — a front-end team and a backend team who either both honor the agreed spec, one honors it while the other quietly changes it, or both defect and build incompatible workarounds requiring maximum rework. Its key leadership insight is that the payoff matrix isn't fixed for a leader sitting above both teams the way it is for the teams themselves: a leader can change meeting cadence, install processes that catch defections early, and convert isolated "one-shot" projects into "repeated games" where cooperation becomes the rational choice because the teams know they'll work together again. Practical recommendations include actively monitoring whether teams are actually following agreed specs rather than assuming goodwill or motivation is sufficient, and creating basic visibility mechanisms — like a shared weekly dashboard sync — that remove the uncertainty driving teams toward self-protective defection in the first place.
points: The Prisoner's Dilemma, developed by RAND Corporation game theorists during the Cold War, shows that when two parties make rational, self-protective decisions independently, the combined outcome can be worse for both than if they had simply trusted each other.

Mapped onto engineering teams: when both a front-end and backend team honor an agreed API spec, that's the best combined outcome — but it only works if each side is confident the other won't quietly change course, which is exactly the confidence cross-team projects usually lack.

A leader sitting above both teams has power the teams themselves don't: the payoff matrix isn't fixed for them, and they can change meeting cadence, install processes that catch early defections, and build interpersonal trust between teams outside the project itself.

Converting a project from a "one-shot game" into a "repeated game" — where the same teams know they'll work together again — makes cooperation the rational choice and makes trust easier to build over time.

A simple visibility mechanism, like a shared weekly sync where both teams look at the same project dashboard together, can be enough to remove the uncertainty that drives teams toward defensive, workaround-building behavior.
quotes: Most teams call this a communication problem, or a trust problem, but what's really running it under the hood is the Prisoner's Dilemma.

The key insight of the Prisoner's Dilemma is this: when people make rational, self-protective decisions independently, they can add up to be the worse outcome for both parties than if they had simply trusted each other.

Both teams defect: both the teams build workarounds and diverge from the original spec, and when they finally meet, they find their implementations poles apart. This is the worst outcome because it requires the maximum rework.

As a leader who has visibility into both teams, and power to influence their goals and priorities, you can change how often the teams meet and coordinate. You can also set processes that catch defections or silos that lead to them in the first place.

One-shot games are harder to fix as they only involve "one" shot at the coordination or project. This is where the rational choice is typically deflection. Repeated games are those where the same teams work together again, and cooperation becomes the more rational choice.

Pay attention to the dynamics in the team - how they commit, how they coordinate with other teams, do they follow the agreed specs and terms, etc. Don't just assume that 'motivating' the team will be enough for them to build trust with each other.
